versions.text:
The Wren had spent two winters in Grandpa Aurel's shed, ever since the March storm tore her loose from the dock and threw her against the rocks below Harrowby Point. His knees had already ended his fishing the autumn before. He would stand in the shed doorway with his coffee and study her the way he studied a crossword.

On the first fair morning of April, we hauled her onto sawhorses. Grandpa was sure the bow had taken the worst of it, and the bow was scraped, and one oarlock had worked loose, but when I ran my hand along her underside I found a split running half the length of the keel. Aunt Bea claims he won her in a race, and Mother has always called her a wedding present. Under the middle seat, though, cut into the cedar, were two sets of initials, his and his father's, beside a date from the summer he turned twelve.

At supper the family argued about her. Mother thought she would make a handsome bed for tomatoes by the front steps. Aunt Bea had already asked Mr. Tolland next door what he would pay. I wanted to row her across the lake to school each morning. Grandpa listened, then took down a faded program from the Harrowby regatta, the year he was sixteen, with the Wren listed among the entries.

So we rebuilt her for the race. In May we steamed new oak into the keel, and Mr. Tolland, who had hoped to buy her, lent us his clamps instead. Mother planted her tomatoes in an old washtub. The school crossing could wait for autumn, Grandpa said; the regatta was in June, and his knees could manage the steering seat if my arms managed the oars.

We finished fourth. I had expected to feel mostly relief when it was over, but that was the wrong word for it. There is a ribbon tacked above her bow now, and I find reasons to bring every visitor out to the shed. When anyone asks who repaired the keel, I tell them, slowly, and leave out none of the steps.

The Wren had spent two winters in Grandpa Aurel's shed, ever since the March storm caught him a mile out and he rowed home through it with his hands bleeding. He gave up fishing that week and sold his nets. The boat herself came through without a scratch, yet he would stand in the shed doorway with his coffee and study her the way he studied a crossword.

In April we hauled her onto sawhorses. Grandpa was sure the damp had got into the keel, but the keel rang solid under his knuckles; it was a plank by the rear seat that had gone soft as bread. Aunt Bea repeated her story that someone handed him the boat to settle a debt, and Mother has always believed he and his father built her. Grandpa laughed and showed us a name half-buried under the paint inside the stern, Ezra Pell, a fisherman who had moved south to his daughter's and asked only a fair price for her, far less than she was worth.

At supper the family argued about her. Aunt Bea wanted to sell her to Mr. Tolland next door. A woman from the county museum had written to say they collected lake boats. I thought she still had one more race in her. Mother said nothing, then went out and studied the bare strip of yard by the front steps.

So the Wren became a garden. Grandpa drilled holes in her bottom for drainage, which he said was the first time in fifty years he had made a boat leak on purpose, and we filled her with soil and tomato seedlings. Mr. Tolland decided he liked her better this way. The museum got a polite letter and a photograph.

By August the tomatoes had tangled around the seat where Grandpa used to sit. He keeps his coffee mug on her bow now and calls her the slowest boat on the lake. I had worried I would feel a little sad each time I passed her, but mostly I grin. Visitors ask whether she is sinking, and Grandpa tells them she is only gardening.

The Wren had spent two winters in Grandpa Aurel's shed, ever since the March storm. I was out in her alone that afternoon when the wind came across the water, and I still remember the oars twisting out of my hands. Grandpa reached me in Mr. Tolland's motorboat. I have stayed off the lake since then, and he would stand in the shed doorway with his coffee and study her the way he studied a crossword.

In April we hauled her onto sawhorses and scraped off the old paint, and the cedar underneath turned out to be in fair shape. Grandpa was sure the stern had cracked when she struck the dock, but the stern was whole; the real crack ran up from the waterline near the bow. While we worked he told me about his wedding. Aunt Bea says he bought the Wren from a fisherman, and Mother insists he won her rowing. Grandpa said my grandmother's brothers carried the boat down to the water the morning after the ceremony, with ribbons still tied to the oarlocks.

At supper the family argued about her. Grandpa wanted to fix her for the June regatta, and Mother suggested I could row her to school once the weather turned. I said I would rather take the bus the long way around. Mr. Tolland had offered to buy her twice already, and Aunt Bea said a boat belonged with someone who would use it.

So the Wren went next door. Mr. Tolland paid more than Aunt Bea asked and spent May sealing the crack by the bow. Grandpa gave him the old oars too, and the ribbons, which had faded to the color of straw. The regatta came and went, and Grandpa watched it from the porch.

Now I can see her from my window, tied at Mr. Tolland's dock, and in the evenings he rows her out past the point. Mother told me I would feel relieved once she was gone, and some days I do. More often I stand at the window after dark, looking at the empty place at our own dock and wishing I had asked to sit in her one last time.

The Wren had spent two winters in Grandpa Aurel's shed, ever since the March storm flattened the Pell boatyard and every boat stored in it. She had been out on loan that week, so she alone survived of all the boats old Pell had built by hand. Grandpa would stand in the shed doorway with his coffee and study her the way he studied a crossword.

In April we hauled her onto sawhorses. Grandpa was sure a plank by the rear seat had rotted, but it was sound; the only real trouble was the left oarlock, which had pulled a fair way out of its socket and wobbled at a touch. While we worked, I asked about her history. Mother had heard she was a wedding gift, and Aunt Bea believed someone had handed her over to clear a debt. Grandpa just tapped a small brass plate on the middle seat: Harrowby Regatta, Single Sculls, First Place, with his name and a year beneath it.

At supper the family argued about her. Aunt Bea wanted to sell her to Mr. Tolland, and Mother pictured her full of tomatoes by the front steps. I hoped Grandpa would race her one more time. Then he set a letter beside his plate from the county museum, which had heard about the boatyard and wanted the one surviving Pell boat for its new lake gallery.

So in June two men in gloves drove her away to Calder in a padded van. Grandpa tightened the oarlock himself the night before. Mr. Tolland admitted the museum would look after her better than he could, and Mother planted her tomatoes in a washtub.

I went to see her in September. She sits under soft lights now, beside a card about the storm and a photograph of Grandpa at nineteen holding up the brass plate. Someone might expect me to swell with pride, but what I mostly felt was the weight of two winters lifting off my shoulders. Nobody has to keep her dry anymore or argue about what she is for.

The Wren had spent two winters in Grandpa Aurel's shed before the March storm brought her out. The storm washed away half a mile of the shore road, so the school bus had to go the long way around the lake, an hour each direction. Grandpa stood in the shed doorway with his coffee, studying her the way he studied a crossword, and one morning he called me in.

We hauled her onto sawhorses. Grandpa was sure the oarlocks would be the trouble, but they turned in his fingers like new; the real damage was a hole in the stern the size of a fist, where something had gnawed through. Grandpa, who tries to be fair, told her story to all of us at once. Mother had always assumed he and his father built her, and Aunt Bea thought he had bought her. In fact a neighbor had once borrowed forty dollars from him, and when the man moved away, he left the Wren tied at Grandpa's dock with a note that read, “We’re square.”

At supper the family argued about her. Aunt Bea said Mr. Tolland would pay well. Mother suggested the county museum. My cousin Pim wanted to fill her with soil and grow pumpkins. Grandpa unfolded a map and drew a pencil line across the lake from our dock to the landing below the school.

So the Wren became my ferry. We patched the stern with oak, and by mid-April I was rowing the mile to school each morning, twenty minutes against the hour the bus took. Mr. Tolland, who had wanted her, lent me his spare life jacket. The museum could have her someday, Grandpa said, but not yet.

The other students found it very funny to watch me tie up at the landing, and I laughed along for a day or two. What stays with me is something else. Each morning Grandpa stands at the kitchen window with his coffee while I push off, and each afternoon I find the stern patch oiled and the seat wiped dry, though he has never once mentioned doing it. I raise an oar to the window every time.
